metadata.notes: Closed all eight primary occurrence/date/location corroboration gaps using source-led replacements, with exact UTC, station, report age and meteorology caveats. Not human fact-checked for publication; remaining 717 uncorroborated alternate cores and all 366 approval/media gates remain.

reviews.title_before: Winter Weather — MISSOULA / BITTERROOT VALLEYS, Montana
reviews.title_after: Freezing rain leaves much of southern Michigan coated in ice
reviews.location_after: Southeastern and southwestern Lower Michigan, United States
reviews.core_fact: A major February 22, 2023 freezing-rain and sleet event iced southern Lower Michigan, downing trees and power lines and causing substantial outages; snow fell farther north.
reviews.source_dependence: Detroit and Grand Rapids NWS case studies use separate local observations but remain within NOAA and often share spotter and utility reports; independent instrument verification and utility records remain to be checked.
reviews.unverified_cautions: NWS Detroit documents more than 500,000 utility outages and roughly 3,000 downed wires as utility-sourced, time-varying event reports, not weather-gauge values. Ice totals vary by location and time. February 21 adjacent snow post is from a different 2013 Wichita storm.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original Michigan icing-type transect with surface temperatures, warm nose, observed icing range and outage timing.

reviews.title_after: Satellite sensors capture explosive Great Plains wildfires
reviews.location_after: Kansas–Oklahoma border and Texas Panhandle, United States
reviews.core_fact: VIIRS on Suomi NPP captured fires raging along the Kansas–Oklahoma border on March 6, 2017; dry fuels, low humidity and strong winds contributed to destructive regional wildfire spread.
reviews.source_dependence: NASA satellite detections document March 6 burning directly, while NWS Amarillo supplies dated ground fire-weather and response information. Their meteorological analyses share regional NOAA observing infrastructure, but visual and response observations differ.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The March 6 VIIRS acquisition was at 19:24 UTC (early afternoon Central time). Distinguish separately named Starbuck, Perryton and other fires: acreage totals differ by agency, burn complex, date and mapping method. A satellite hot spot is not a precise ignition timestamp. Third-party photography is not automatically public domain.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original March 6 VIIRS thermal detections above surface wind/RH and mapped wildfire area boundaries.

reviews.title_after: An extraordinarily deep trough brings thundersnow to Mexico
reviews.secondary_publisher: The Weather Channel contemporary meteorological analysis
reviews.core_fact: On March 9, 2016, high-elevation areas of central Mexico experienced unusual winter weather including reported thundersnow at Zacatecas airport, during a deep anomalous upper-level trough that contributed to exceptional March conditions across North America.
reviews.source_dependence: The AMS analysis is based on reanalysis/physical diagnosis, while contemporaneous Weather Channel and Washington Post independently report the March 9 Zacatecas thundersnow, generally using the same airport observing system.
reviews.unverified_cautions: A published AMS analysis examines 7–11 March and 500-hPa anomalies near nine standard deviations below a particular climatology; this statistic is NOT a 9-sigma rainfall or daily snowfall reading. Confirm METAR/thunder observation timing before final wording. The downstream March 2016 Louisiana flood must not be conflated with the March 8 1998 Elba flood or March 10 California event.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original reanalysis 500-hPa height/anomaly panel centered over Mexico with March 9 Zacatecas airport weather chronology.

reviews.title_after: The tropical depression that became Maysak develops east of Pohnpei
reviews.location_after: Western North Pacific east of Pohnpei, Federated States of Micronesia
reviews.core_fact: JMA's post-season record begins the tropical depression precursor of Maysak east of Pohnpei at 12 UTC on March 26, 2015; it became a tropical storm on March 27 UTC and a typhoon on March 29 UTC.
reviews.source_dependence: The JMA best-track annual report and HKO retrospective are separate regional agencies but both draw on the overlapping western North Pacific analysis/observing network; dates and lifecycle-stage definitions, not independently measured peak winds, are the corroborated issue.
reviews.unverified_cautions: March 26 is the JMA tropical-DEPRESSION start in UTC, NOT Maysak's naming or typhoon-intensity date. HKO dates formation to the morning of March 27 in local Hong Kong time; clock/date conventions and operational genesis definitions differ. Digital Typhoon marks best-track data start March 26 12 UTC but its listed tropical-cyclone 'Birth' March 27 18 UTC, so do not conflate those definitions. NOAA's previous Guam NCEI zone episode date did NOT establish a March 26 typhoon near Guam. Later impacts and wind speeds are not March 26 values.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original western Pacific JMA best-track timeline showing depression genesis March 26 UTC then later naming, intensity and island impacts.

reviews.title_after: A giant hailstone falls near Potter, Nebraska
reviews.location_after: Potter, Cheyenne County, Nebraska, United States
reviews.secondary_publisher: Nebraska Game and Parks Commission archive (Nebraskaland, 1996)
reviews.core_fact: On July 6, 1928, a giant hailstone reportedly measured 17 inches in circumference and weighed about 1.5 pounds near Potter, Nebraska, according to a contemporary historical account and a later state records compilation.
reviews.source_dependence: The 1930 Nature archive and later Nebraska state historical weather records repeat the same original 1928 hail measurement and are not two separately measured stones. Strong event/date plausibility does not clear precise maximum diameter.
reviews.unverified_cautions: A 1930 Nature account and the Nebraska archive preserve the historic report; the diameter is inconsistently stated as 5.5 or 7 inches in retrospective summaries, and a 17-inch circumference does not mechanically imply seven-inch maximum diameter for an irregular stone. DO NOT say it is today's world-record hailstone or equate the historic reported measurement to modern calibrated observing methods. Original stone and image provenance require item-level review.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original dimensioned historic hailstone silhouette based on reported 17-inch circumference beside later modern storm-report standards.

reviews.title_after: An 1838 tornado sweeps past Providence toward Somerset
reviews.location_after: South of Providence, Rhode Island, and near Somerset, Massachusetts, United States
reviews.secondary_publisher: Original 1838–39 tornado account by Robert Hare and Zachariah Allen (Biodiversity Heritage Library)
reviews.core_fact: On the afternoon of August 30, 1838, a tornado passed south of Providence, Rhode Island, and into portions of the surrounding New England region; early scientific observers documented its damage and motion.
reviews.source_dependence: NWS's dated historical digest and the publicly cataloged original 1838/1839 written observations confirm event identity. The weather archive may rely on the same early observations and does not provide independent surveyed EF ratings.
reviews.unverified_cautions: Contemporaneous reports use premodern 'whirlwind' terminology and historical witness accounts, not a modern Doppler or post-1950 path survey. Avoid assigning an EF/F rating or exact modern track length and distinguish Providence, Rhode Island from Somerset, Massachusetts. Damage and injury totals in retrospectives are not fully audited.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original reconstruction of 1838 Providence–Somerset witness bearings on modern coastline terrain with explicit uncertainty cones.

reviews.title_after: Corpus Christi begins an eight-day run of daily record highs
reviews.location_after: Corpus Christi, Nueces County, Texas, United States
reviews.secondary_publisher: USDA Weekly Weather and Crop Bulletin (Oct. 2005)
reviews.core_fact: September 22, 2005 began a streak of eight consecutive days on which Corpus Christi tied or exceeded its calendar-day high-temperature records, extending through September 29, according to Texas A&M and the USDA climate summary.
reviews.source_dependence: Texas A&M and USDA separately authored summaries of a common official station daily temperature series, so the publications are distinct but not independent thermometers.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The eight-day run is retrospective, beginning September 22 but only known after September 29; it is NOT eight successive all-time absolute heat records. Corpus Christi's listed high on September 22 was 99°F at the climate station, whereas larger regional maxima were observed later. Rita affected the Gulf Coast during the same week but is not itself the selected September 22 event; avoid attributing evacuation mortality to heat without specific evidence. NOAA station data are reused by multiple publishers.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original Sept22–29 Corpus Christi daily Tmax bars with date-specific daily records and Hurricane Rita's passage shown only as synoptic context.

reviews.title_before: High Wind — FOOTHILLS OF THE BLUE MOUNTAINS, Oregon
reviews.title_after: An exceptionally early September snowfall reaches central Illinois
reviews.location_after: Central Illinois, upper Mississippi Valley and western Great Lakes, United States
reviews.core_fact: On September 25, 1942, an unusually early snowstorm produced measurable snowfall across parts of Illinois and the upper Midwest. NWS Lincoln reports most central Illinois totals accumulated on the 25th, with 2 inches reported at Galesburg and Minonk.
reviews.source_dependence: NWS Lincoln and La Crosse case retrospectives cover partly separate regions and historical official station reports, but both belong to NOAA and draw on early station/observer logs. An independent local retrospective also corroborates the Quad Cities Sep25 record.
reviews.unverified_cautions: The 1942 storm spanned September 24–26 across multiple states. La Crosse's station-specific earliest measurable snowfall is recorded September 26 (not automatically Sep 25), while central Illinois amounts mostly fell the 25th. Historic daily cooperative measurements can be from morning observation periods; do not call all Upper Midwest totals a September 25 calendar-day amount.
reviews.graphic_concept: Original September 24–26 Midwest snowfall swath with day-of-occurrence shading and selected station historical daily totals.

editorial_deferrals.decision: Only the JMA 12 UTC March26 precursor TD date is supported. HKO's 27 March local formation and Digital Typhoon's later named-storm birth are different lifecycle/clock definitions. Never call it March26 typhoon.
Only central Illinois and specific stations are dated to September 25; do not shift La Crosse's September 26 station total back a day.
Exclude any purported 7-inch diameter or present-day world record without primary calibration and source measurement reconciliation.
